candidates.title: The half-time line is a famous misattribution
candidates.detail: Ted closes his half-time speech with the line about the day the risk of staying tight in a bud became more painful than the risk of blossoming. The line is one of the most widely circulated quotations in the English-speaking self-help world and is almost universally credited to Anais Nin. It is not hers. It was written in 1979 by Elizabeth Appell, then director of public relations at John F. Kennedy University in Orinda, California, for the cover of a quarterly class-schedule brochure; she published under the name Lassie Benton at the time and the brochure carried no byline, which is how the attribution drifted. The Official Anais Nin Blog, run by Sky Blue Press (her publisher), has said the line appears nowhere in Nin's work and credited Appell after she produced the 1979 brochure page in 2013. REVIEWER: two things need separating. (a) Is the line in the episode at all - yes, two independent reviews report it. (b) Does Ted name Nin on screen, or is 'attributed to Anais Nin' the reviewer's own framing? But Why Tho quotes the speech as ending with a quote 'attributed to Anais Nin'; Ready Steady Cut's recap instead credits Elizabeth Appell in its own voice. I could not open a transcript to settle it (scrapsfromtheloft returns 403). Treat the on-screen attribution as unsettled and write the card so it holds either way. This is the exact same shape as the Whitman sign in S1E8 and should be flagged as such.
candidates.moment: Two down at half-time in front of a half-empty ground, Ted stops talking about the football and talks about himself instead, then ends on the bud-and-blossom line.

candidates.title: The title inverts a 300-year-old French joke
candidates.detail: 'Riches of Embarrassment' flips 'an embarrassment of riches', which is a calque of the French 'embarras des richesses' and enters English through John Ozell's translation of a 1726 comedy by Leonor Jean Christine Soulas d'Allainval titled 'L'Embarras des richesses'. Sources differ on the translation's date: 1738 is the figure usually repeated, but at least one source argues Ozell registered it in 1735. The original sense is being encumbered by having too much to choose from. The episode inverts it into embarrassment itself as the abundance. Worth noting for the reviewer that Ted Lasso episode titles are habitually wordplay, but I have found no interview confirming intent here - the etymology is solid, the authorial intent is inference.

candidates.title: Embarrassment is not a malfunction; it is the system working
candidates.detail: The sociologist Erving Goffman published 'Embarrassment and Social Organization' in the American Journal of Sociology in November 1956 (vol. 62, no. 3, pp. 264-271). His argument runs against the intuition that embarrassment is a personal failure: it arises when a person is felt to have projected incompatible definitions of themselves to the people present, and it happens at predictable structural points where incompatible principles of social organisation meet. Embarrassment, on Goffman's account, has a social function - it forestalls the conflict between those principles. REVIEWER: this is an interpretive pairing, not something the episode names. The episode does not mention Goffman. Judge relevance accordingly; the honest framing on a card is 'here is a thinker who took this seriously', not 'the show is referencing Goffman'.
candidates.moment: The whole episode: the photograph of Ted eating alone, Jane staging her worst behaviour for a paying audience, Alice calling her own players embarrassing, and a half-empty stand watching all of it.

candidates.title: Why a women's team playing at Nelson Road is loaded
candidates.detail: The episode turns on the Lady Greyhounds playing at Nelson Road and the stands being half empty. The real history behind that: on Boxing Day 1920 the Dick, Kerr Ladies drew a crowd estimated at 53,000 to Goodison Park, with more unable to get in. On 5 December 1921 the Football Association banned women's football from grounds affiliated to the FA, on the stated grounds that the game was quite unsuitable for females and ought not to be encouraged. Women's football was pushed into public parks for the next fifty years. The FA rescinded the ruling at its Annual General Meeting on 24 June 1971 at the Great Western Royal Hotel in Paddington, following an FA Council vote on 19 January 1970. So 'a women's team playing at the men's ground' is not a neutral fact in England - it was illegal for half a century, and the empty seats are the ban's long tail. REVIEWER: the FA's own heritage page is the primary source for the dates and the wording. Please check whether the episode itself states that this is the first women's match at Nelson Road - one recap (Ready Steady Cut) reports Keeley saying so; another (Nerd Alert) does not confirm it. Do not put words in Keeley's mouth if it cannot be corroborated.

candidates.title: The woman who plays Jane wrote the episode about Jane's play
candidates.detail: Phoebe Walsh is credited as the writer of 'Riches of Embarrassment' - her fourth writing credit on the series - and she is also the actor who has played Jane Payne since season one, and appears in this episode's guest cast. So the episode in which Jane writes and performs a one-woman show about her own worst behaviour was written by the performer who plays her. Walsh has been on the writing staff across the run (story editor and executive story editor credits) and shares in the show's writing Emmys and WGA awards. candidates.title: An apology that rewrites the facts is not an apology
candidates.detail: Jane's one-woman show is presented as an apology - she stages her own trial for having lied to Beard about being pregnant - but it also invents things that did not happen, including a version of Ted she sleeps with. There is a philosophical literature on exactly this gap. Nick Smith's 'I Was Wrong: The Meanings of Apologies' (Cambridge University Press, 2008) sets out what he calls a categorical apology, and one of its required elements is a corroborated factual record: the apologiser has to identify the harm with precision, not gesture at it. An apology that improves the story in the telling fails that condition however sincerely it is felt. REVIEWER: Smith's framework is well documented; the risk here is over-reading the episode. Recaps agree the show is framed as an apology, that it fictionalises, and that Beard tries to stop it and cannot because it is transferring to the West End. Do not assert the show's own verdict on Jane beyond that.

candidates.title: Ted has seen this before, and this time he acts in week five
candidates.detail: Alice Chilton's behaviour in this episode - resentment at being overlooked, an inability to say what she actually feels, and cruelty to players as the outlet - is widely read by critics as the show running the Nate Shelley arc again. Christopher Orr in the New York Times noted the resemblance to later-season Nate while praising Tanya Reynolds. The structural difference is the point: with Nate, Ted's response to warning signs was warmth and patience, and it took three seasons and a defection to a rival club to resolve. Here Ted suspends Alice for a match after a single episode of it, and the suspension runs into the Christmas break. REVIEWER: the Nate comparison is critical opinion, held by several outlets, not a stated fact - frame it as a reading, and attribute it. The suspension and its length are reported consistently across recaps.

candidates.title: The barbecue metaphor, and why it is an argument about coaching
candidates.detail: Ted answers Alice's approach with a barbecue metaphor: good barbecue is cooked low and slow, and prodding the meat constantly makes it tough. It is a Kansas City man's version of a coaching philosophy - the claim that pressure applied continuously is not the same as pressure applied well, and that some results cannot be hurried. The half-time speech reportedly returns to his own experience of learning to barbecue. REVIEWER: the metaphor is reported by three independent recaps in compatible terms. What varies is exactly where it lands (a conversation with Alice, and/or the half-time speech). Please pin down which, or keep the card vague enough to be true either way. Do not reproduce the wording.

candidates.title: Sold out on paper, half empty in the seats, a record on television
candidates.detail: Keeley gets the match to a sellout by discounting and giving tickets away, and Zelda Southport buys in bulk - and then roughly half the ground sits empty on the day, because a ticket sold is not a person in a seat. After the loss, Boots tells Keeley the broadcast audience hit record levels. The episode sets two different measures of whether a thing succeeded against each other in the same afternoon. REVIEWER: the sellout-versus-empty-seats detail is reported by But Why Tho and the record-viewership beat is on the Wikipedia page and in the Nerd Alert recap. I have not found a figure for either and would not want one invented. Zelda Southport is Tracey Ullman's season-four character, introduced the previous episode as the managing partner of a firm investing in women's sport.

candidates.title: An episode about embarrassment ends on an own goal
candidates.detail: Richmond go two down, equalise through Gemma and Margy, and then lose in the closing moments when Niamh puts it into her own net - reported as a 3-2 defeat. Football has no more publicly embarrassing way to lose, and the episode has spent forty minutes arguing that embarrassment is not worth much next to having tried. The ending declines to let the argument off easily. REVIEWER: sources agree on the shape (0-2 down, two back, lost late to an own goal or deflection) and Wikipedia gives 3-2. The competition is less certain - Ready Steady Cut calls it an FA Cup tie, other sources just say a home match against Chelsea. Do not assert the competition unless you can corroborate it.

candidates.title: Ted eating alone, and the difference between being alone and being lonely
candidates.detail: The episode opens with two players photographing Ted eating a hot dog by himself and circulating it, on the assumption that a man alone must be a man in trouble; Ted maintains he is fine. Hannah Arendt drew the distinction the episode is fumbling toward. In 'Ideology and Terror' (1953, later the closing chapter of 'The Origins of Totalitarianism') she separates isolation, loneliness and solitude: solitude is where thinking happens, a person keeping company with themselves, while loneliness is the state of being deserted even among others. On her account you can be alone without being lonely, and lonely in a crowd. REVIEWER: Arendt is not referenced by the episode - this is an interpretive pairing, same caveat as the Goffman candidate. The Arendt distinction itself is well documented but please verify against a source that quotes her text rather than a summary, and keep any quotation short.
